title: ר' אבא בר זימנא

paragraphs: Rabbi Abba bar Zimna, in Rabbi Eliezer Ze'ira’s name: “If the earlier ones were angels.” So writes Yuchasin. Indeed Tosafot, first chapter of Shabbat (12, end of b), write: “In Bereshit Rabbah: Rabbi Abba bar Zimna, in Rabbi Eliezer Ze'ira’s name: If the earlier ones,” etc. The new Talmud editions did not correct it. Yuchasin further writes: “Eliezer Ze'ira was a great sage, and his student, the wise and pious Rabbi Abba bar Zimuna.” But he relied on a broken reed: the reading in Tosafot that he spoke in Eliezer Ze'ira’s name. “Eliezer” is a scribal error. Tosafot took their words from Bereshit Rabbah, intending Chayyei Sarah, section 60: “Rabbi Abba bar Zimna said to Rabbi Ze'ira: If the earlier ones,” etc. So too Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of chapter 5 of Shekalim, end of Rosh Hashanah, and beginning of Demai. In Babylonian Shabbat 112b: Rabbi Zeira said—“Rava said” is our reading, a scribal error which should be—Rabbi Abba bar Zimuna said in Rabbi’s name (“Rabbi” is absent from our Gemara): “If the earlier ones,” etc. In the Jerusalem Talmud, end of chapter Sheloshah She'akhalu: Rabbi Yonah and Rabbi Abba b.Z. in Rabbi Ze'ira’s name. In that chapter, mishnah 3, Rabbi Abba bar Zamina attended Ze'ira and mixed him a cup; in chapter Kelal Gadol, halakhah 2, he bathed with him. Yuchasin reports that Rabbi Abba b.Z. told Rabbi Abbahu that one must mention the occasion—that is, Shabbat or a festival—in the third blessing, since Rabbi Ze'ira took account of it. End quotation. I saw in the Jerusalem Talmud, chapter Keitzad Mevarkhin, mishnah 1: “Should one mention the occasion in it? Rabbi Abba b.Z. said: Rabbi Ze'ira would mention the occasion. Rabbi Yirmeyah said: Since Rabbi Ze'ira took account of it, we must take account of it.” End quotation. Thus the report that he spoke to Rabbi Abbahu is a scribal error. The truth bears witness to itself: Rabbi Ze'ira was Rabbi Abba b.Z.’s teacher; “Eliezer” is a scribal error, and none of the earlier writers took care to correct it.

Yuchasin writes: Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin, chapter 3, halakhah 6: Rabbi Abba b.Z. lived with a gentile in Rome. (This is a scribal error; it should read “was sewing for an Aramean.”) The gentile told him, “Eat carrion; otherwise I will kill you.” He replied, “If you wish, kill me; I will not eat.” The gentile said, “Who told you? Had you eaten, I would have killed you: either be a Jew or an Aramean.” (So too Shevi'it, chapter 4, halakhah 2. It concludes: had Rabbi Abba b.Z. heard the rabbis’ words that in private one should transgress rather than be killed for all offenses except idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and bloodshed, he would have eaten.) Rosh, chapter Ein Ma'amidin, writes that presumably it was privately in the house, but he wished to be stringent with himself. End quotation. (On that basis, the Jerusalem Talmud’s statement that had he heard the rabbis’ words he would have eaten is difficult. Whence do we know he had not heard? Perhaps he heard but was stringent with himself; וק״ל [abbreviation uncertain].) In R. Avdimi of Haifa’s name, and Rabbi Dostai (see Chizkiyah); in Rabbi Yitzchak’s name (Jerusalem Talmud, Beitzah, chapter 2; Shevi'it, beginning of chapter 9). Rabbi Yose bar Zamina—perhaps his brother.
